question: A 40-year-old PLHIV presents with severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. His CD4 count is 45 cells/μL. Which opportunistic infection is MOST likely and which investigation should be prioritised?

answers.text: Cerebral toxoplasmosis — order CT brain with contrast

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Toxoplasmosis typically presents with focal neurological deficits and ring-enhancing lesions. Meningism (neck stiffness, photophobia) without focal deficits points more towards cryptococcal meningitis.

answers.text: Cryptococcal meningitis — order India ink staining and cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) on CSF

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cryptococcal meningitis classically presents with sub-acute meningism at CD4 < 100 cells/μL. The diagnostic tests of choice are India ink staining (rapid, inexpensive) and CSF/serum cryptococcal antigen (high sensitivity and specificity).

answers.text: TB meningitis — order CSF AFB smear and culture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TB meningitis is a possibility but the presentation (severe meningism, very low CD4) with no focal signs makes cryptococcal meningitis more likely at this CD4 level. CrAg testing should not be deferred.

answers.text: Viral encephalitis — order CSF PCR for HSV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HSV encephalitis is less strongly associated with low CD4 counts and typically presents with focal neurological signs and fever. The clinical picture here is more consistent with cryptococcal meningitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Apply symptom-CD4 reasoning: at CD4 < 100 cells/μL, fungal OIs (Cryptococcus, PCP) dominate. Meningism without focal deficits strongly favours cryptococcal meningitis over toxoplasmosis or TB meningitis.
Excellent clinical reasoning. At CD4 < 100 cells/μL, meningism without focal deficits = cryptococcal meningitis until proven otherwise. CrAg has >90% sensitivity and is the priority test.
